The Financial Markets Dealers Association (FMDA), in its November pre-MPC analysis, projected a 60 per cent probability that the committee would hold the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) at 23 per cent, against a 40 per cent probability of a rate cut of up to 50 basis points.
According to the report, although Nigeria’s headline inflation moderated further to 14.06 per cent in October from 14.63 per cent in September, the rebound in monthly inflation and renewed pressure on the foreign exchange market could discourage the committee from reducing interest rates further.
FMDA noted that month-on-month inflation accelerated to 0.43 per cent in October from 0.06 per cent in September, driven largely by increases in energy and transportation costs, which rose by 1.74 per cent and 1.86 per cent respectively. Food inflation stood at 19.13 per cent, while core inflation was 10.78 per cent.
It said the real policy rate of about 8.9 percentage points provides room for a rate reduction, but the mixed inflation outlook makes the decision finely balanced.
The report also identified the recent depreciation of the naira and the decline in external reserves as factors that could influence the committee’s decision. The naira weakened to N1,377 to the dollar at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) on November 19, from N1,363 the previous day, representing a depreciation of about one per cent.
Similarly, weekly foreign exchange inflows declined sharply to $808 million from $2.48 billion in the preceding week, while gross external reserves stood at $54.76 billion as of November 17, about $500 million below the peak recorded on October 27.
The association further noted that liquidity in the banking system had tightened, with the system balance declining to N4.47 trillion on November 20 from N7.37 trillion at the end of October, as Open Market Operations (OMO) sales outpaced repayments.
Another consideration is the external monetary policy environment, particularly the expected interest rate decision of the United States Federal Reserve. FMDA noted that no major central bank had reduced interest rates since September, while a 25-basis-point hike by the US Federal Reserve in December was fully priced into the market.
It noted that the gap between Nigeria’s MPR and the upper end of the US Federal Reserve’s policy rate range had narrowed from 22.50 percentage points at the September MPC meeting to 19 percentage points.
According to the association, further narrowing of the interest rate differential could weaken the attractiveness of Nigerian assets to foreign portfolio investors and increase pressure on capital flows.
On the domestic financial market, the report observed that the transmission of previous monetary policy adjustments had been uneven. While treasury bill yields had repriced downward following the September rate reduction, bond yields had barely adjusted, declining by just six basis points.
Average treasury bill yields declined by 122 basis points, while the stop rate on the 364-day treasury bill remained between 15.80 and 15.90 per cent. The one-month treasury bill yield, however, rose to 20.46 per cent, while the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rate at 20 per cent continued to anchor overnight interest rates.
The FMDA said the September rate reset had brought the MPR to a level where the market was already positioned, meaning another cut would represent a more significant move towards monetary easing. It also recalled that a member of the MPC had cautioned that the September reduction was not a shift towards an accommodative monetary policy stance.
The November meeting comes after the MPC reduced the benchmark interest rate by 350 basis points to 23 per cent at its September meeting.
